Tests as data

Ensuring AI-generated code does what we want

Automated testing in the age of AI coding assistants is problematic: when AI agents write both production and test code, developers risk losing the assurance that automated tests protect against functional errors. I make three claims: (1) when AI writes the code, developers become its customers; (2) therefore customer tests, not developer tests, become the primary contract between humans and AI; (3) moving that contract into test data rather than test code makes it easier to protect it from unexpected modifications by coding agents. All of this optimizes for human-readable tests that establish a contract between humans and AI. While in the past DSL parsers and custom test runners were expensive to write and maintain, now AI makes them cheap. I build on established practices: customer-oriented acceptance tests from Extreme Programming, test DSLs from Fit and specification by example, tabular tests from Go, and readable textual representations of application state from approval testing.

Introduction

Problems with AI-generated code

In early 2026, I conducted interviews with 26 developers working for an organization that was heavily invested in developing with AI coding agents. One of my questions was “do you trust our tests?” After all, the developers were from Thoughtworks, and Thoughtworks prides itself on the quality and thoroughness of our testing. Unfortunately, the developers invariably answered “Well… I don’t trust our tests that much! Because even if I review the tests when they are initially generated, as new features get added, the AI refactors both existing code and existing tests, so I’m no longer confident that the tests are still ensuring the right behaviour”.

This got me thinking. As we learn to get more work done from coding agents, it’s becoming natural that AI writes most, if not all the tests.
